FIVE NIGHT IN SPACE is an educational survival game that puts kids ages 7 to 12 in command of a lunar research base. Over five night shifts, the player watches the base through cameras from a control center, spots failures, and assigns four specialists (an energy engineer and experts in life support, radiation protection, and communications) to repair them. details:
What it does and how it works

FIVE NIGHT IN SPACE is an educational survival game set in a lunar research base. The player is the commander and works from a fixed control center. Over five night shifts (12:00 AM to 6:00 AM), the player watches the base through cameras, spots failures, and assigns four specialists to repair them: an energy engineer and experts in life support, radiation protection, and communications. The player never repairs anything directly, and time runs continuously, so every order has a cost.

Five systems are managed: power, oxygen, radiation shielding, ventilation, and temperature. Failures are random and increase each night. Assigning a task does not mean it is fixed, so the player must confirm on camera. Specialists get tired, work best in their own field, and can fail outside it. After each night, a report shows decisions and consequences.

Benefits and intended impact

Players learn that no engineering decision is free: saving power can leave another system unprotected, and every repair costs time and people. Because failures change each game, kids can fail, see why, and try a new strategy. We want children ages 7 to 12 to leave with one true idea about deep-space survival, and the game can also work in classrooms and for older siblings.

NASA data

We plan to use DONKI for solar activity and space weather alerts, and OSDR for short, plain-language explanations based on astronaut health research. Real data is kept separate from simulation values. Archived records will show their date and source and will never be presented as live.

Tools and technology

  • Gemini: visual design and context.
  • Codex: programming.
  • ChatGPT: idea generation.
  • GitHub: file storage and version control.
  • Programming language or game engine: PYTHON

What makes it creative

It borrows the tension and camera-watching of Five Nights at Freddy’s 3 and the repair tasks of Among Us, but replaces monsters and impostors with real engineering problems. The player directs a crew instead of acting alone, so the trade-offs are about people and time, not only numbers.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: plain language, short explanations of scientific terms, and an easy start.
  • Honest science: a solar event is not the same as the dose an astronaut receives inside a protected habitat, and the game says so.
  • No free choices: every option has a cost.
  • Learning from failure: a loss explains what went wrong instead of only punishing.
  • Accuracy and fun: dramatic gameplay without inventing facts.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
